author: Grand Canyon Times
title: Ciscomani and Pappas introduce AIR CARE for Vets Act to improve respiratory diagnosis
text:
Ciscomani and Pappas introduce AIR CARE for Vets Act to improve respiratory diagnosis
U.S. Representative Juan Ciscomani joined Representative Chris Pappas on July 15 to introduce the AIR CARE for Vets Act, a bill designed to enhance the Department of Veterans Affairs’ ability to diagnose veterans with service-related respiratory conditions. The legislation, known as H.R. 9666, aims to prioritize veteran access to advanced imaging software for diagnosing conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and lung cancer.
The initiative is particularly significant in Arizona’s 6th congressional district, which is home to nearly 80,000 veterans—the ninth largest veteran population by congressional district. Ciscomani said current diagnostic methods rely on whole-lung assessments that may be less sensitive in detecting early-stage disease or localized abnormalities. He also noted that standard procedures like lung biopsies are often painful and invasive.
"Our nation’s heroes deserve access to quality healthcare, including the most up-to-date technology to best diagnose service-related conditions. That’s what the AIR CARE for Vets Act is all about," said Ciscomani. "Under this bill, veterans suffering from respiratory conditions and lung cancer would receive better quality care at the VA through the use of imaging software equipped to properly evaluate their symptoms. Better imaging software means an improved rate of diagnosis, which would save lives by catching issues like lung cancer sooner. The men and women who have sacrificed so much for our country deserve to know they are receiving the highest level of care possible at all stages, starting with quality evaluation of their symptoms." Pappas said, "We owe everything to our veterans, and they deserve access to top-of-the-line health care both during and following their service. Our legislation would establish a pilot program for VA to utilize innovative 4-D lung scanning technology, which improves identification of respiratory disorders and lung disease in veterans. For thousands of veterans living in New Hampshire, exposure to burn pits has significantly increased their chances of developing lung disease and this pilot program will improve the resources and care available to them now and in the years to come."
Leaders from Arizona's veteran community have voiced support for the bill. Tom Murphy, Mayor of Sahuarita and Chair of Congressman Ciscomani's Veterans Advisory Council, said: "As veterans, we face unique healthcare needs because of the challenges and environments we experienced during our time in service. The Air Care Act is a critical step toward meeting that need by expanding access to advanced, noninvasive lung screenings that can provide earlier detection and safer treatment options currently unavailable... We are grateful for Congressman Ciscomani’s leadership in introducing this bipartisan legislation..." Alex Wright (Colonel US Air Force Retired) added: "The Air Care Act will be instrumental in expanding access... By advancing cutting-edge technology... I’m proud of Congressman Ciscomani’s leadership..."
If enacted into law, the AIR CARE for Vets Act would direct VA facilities nationwide over five years through a pilot program using FDA-approved four-dimensional functional lung imaging software intended specifically for identifying respiratory disorders among patients receiving VA care.
The legislation authorizes $5 million annually between Fiscal Year 2027 through Fiscal Year 2031 dedicated toward leasing eligible imaging software from approved developers as well as implementation within VA medical centers.
Ciscomani remains committed toward supporting health initiatives benefiting military personnel; since taking office representing Arizona's 6th District—replacing Ann Kirkpatrick in 2023—he has introduced eighteen bills focused on veterans' issues with four passing through Congress so far, according to his official office. Juan Ciscomani was born in Hermosillo in 1982 before graduating from University of Arizona with a BA degree; he currently resides in Tucson.
